In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

verbal conditioning is a phenomenon which is best explained in terms of a complex interplay of various factors, including the effects of the experimental situation, the effects of the subject’s personality, and the subject’s previous experiences.
the experimental phases should be delineated in terms of the effective transition points, rather than being predefined in a manner which is independent of these points.

the present study indicates that the onset of the experimental phases should be defined in terms not of the number of trials, but of the number of events which effectively delineates the transition from one experimental phase to the next.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the more we can make our procedures and definitions of the experimental situation conform to the natural situation the better our results are going to be, and that we should be as little arbitrary as possible.
we have demonstrated that the experimental phases of the verbal conditioning procedure can be defined in terms that are more meaningful than those customarily employed.
we have demonstrated the feasibility of a procedure that would permit the analysis of conditioning in a manner that is not dependent upon arbitrary assumptions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is not enough to simply define the phases of a verbal conditioning experiment, we must also define when the phases begin and end.
it is not the number of reinforcements, but the number of reinforcements in a row that matters.
we need to rethink our approach to experimental design in verbal conditioning and that the procedure suggested in this paper provides an alternative that is both more valid and less labor intensive.
